KEY POINTS

• This paper demonstrates the feasibility of implementing Geriatric ED programs with targeted support for people living with or at risk for dementia across three distinct health systems in San Francisco. We describe the reach and implementation processes of each program including commonalities, differences, challenges faced, and opportunities for future improvement. • Creating unique care pathways for older adults and those with cognitive impairment in the emergency department (ED) is often guided by health system resources. • Assessing cognition and identifying potential dementia is feasible during an ED visit. • An interprofessional approach to geriatric ED care is essential to sustainability and success.

ABSTRACT 1

Background: 2

Three San Francisco health system emergency departments have developed Geriatric 3

Emergency Department (GED) models of care programs supporting and providing care 4

for emergency department (ED) patients at risk for or living with dementia. Each system 5

recognized: 1) the high proportion of older adult ED patients and those at risk for 6

dementia, 2) the need to identify cognitive impairment in older adult ED patients, 3) the 7

importance of developing approaches to connect older adult ED patients and their care 8

partners with resources and diagnostic specialty services. 9

Methods: 10

We describe how each hospital adopted and implemented pragmatic GED models of 11

care to support and improve care for ED patients at risk or living with dementia. We also 12

report the proportion of ED encounters made by patients with dementia histories and 13

the number of these reached by GED programs. 14

Results: 15

Three San Francisco hospitals (a tertiary care, critical access, and large integrated 16

health system-community ED) independently implemented GED programs to support 17

and enhance emergency care for patients living with dementia. Each uses screening 18

and assessment tools to identify patients at risk for cognitive impairment. Each captures 19

screening and assessment data to facilitate care and resources for post-discharge care, 20

ensuring coordinated transitions and support for older adults. Programs varied by target 21

patient population age and staff and resource allocation to support program goals. Site- 22

specific pathways differed by location, patient populations, and support from geriatrics, 23

Conclusions: 26

Developing GED care interventions that facilitate care for patients at risk of or living with 27

dementia is possible and sustainable when the pathway aligns with health system 28

leadership goals through persistent value demonstration, communication, and 29

promotion. Ultimately, developing and disseminating models of GED care is designed to 30

address geriatric syndromes inclusive of dementia care through continuous quality 31

improvement. 32

INTRODUCTION 33

A majority of older adults in the United States (US) visit the emergency 34

department (ED) each year (61 out of every 100 persons 65+ years in age), 35

representing over 20% of total ED visits.1,2 As the population ages, the lifetime risk of 36

developing dementia also increases such that the incidence of dementia is projected to 37

nearly double in the next 40 years.3 After age 55, men have a 35% and women have a 38

48% risk of developing dementia.3 Unfortunately, persons living with dementia (PLWD) 39

are more than twice as likely to visit the ED compared to other community-dwelling, 40

older adults.4-6 Concurrently, a visit to the ED is a sentinel encounter for common 41

geriatric syndromes including cognitive change.6 ED visits often precede a dementia 42

diagnosis by 6 to 12 months.7,8 43

The ED is an equalizer for access to healthcare as it is one of the few settings 44

where patients of all backgrounds and conditions are seen and cared for, regardless of 45

demography, socioeconomic factors, or conditions.8,9 The ED provides both critical care 46

for those with emergent medical needs and primary care for those that otherwise may 47

have limited access to traditional outpatient care. Many EDs across the country are 48

addressing the special care needs of our aging population by transforming routine care 49

processes and adapting Geriatric Emergency Department (GED) programs.9 These 50

programs and their accreditation are aligned with the new Centers for Medicare and 51

Medicaid Services (CMS) metrics for Age-Friendly Hospitals.10 52

GED accreditation standards for neurocognitive screening and care coordination 53

are recognized as care processes,11 but implementation strategies for different EDs 54

naturally vary in accordance with local needs and context. In San Francisco, 3 EDs 55

need follow-up care coordination, including referrals to primary care or outpatient 59

evaluation by memory care specialists. 60

The objective of this paper is to present 3 pragmatic, age-friendly models of GED 61

care designed for PLWD in San Francisco, CA, USA. We describe each program’s 62

implementation of Age-Friendly healthcare practices including common challenges, 63

variations, and innovative solutions. While two of these programs have been previously 64

described,12,13 this paper will summarize, compare, and contrast the programs, 65

populations reached, challenges, and novel approaches each have taken in their focus 66

on dementia within broader GED care. We describe the population of older adult 67

patients and those with dementia or cognitive impairment diagnoses with visits to these 68

EDs. We also outline how the GED programs evolved their cognitive screening and 69

management strategies to better identify those at risk and their referral processes. 70

Kaiser Permanente San Francisco (KPSF): 85

The Dolby award allowed KPSF to develop risk assessments and workflows for older 86

Dementia patient population seen in EDs: 130

To estimate the potential reach of their programs among patients with prevalent 131

dementia or cognitive impairment, we characterize two populations: Population 1 132

includes all ED patients over 65 years of age. Population 2 includes ED patients over 65 133

years of age with medical diagnoses of dementia or cognitive impairment. We 134

constructed our definition of dementia or cognitive impairment diagnosis codes to be as 135

inclusive as possible by defining an encounter-level indicator of dementia as any 136

dementia or cognitive impairment14-16 in their medical history, problem list, referrals, or 138

billing record available for extraction from health system databases. The complete list of 139

qualifying ICD-10 codes is listed in the appendix. 140

Development of eligibility screening tools and procedures: 147

All three sites began their GED and dementia programs using variants of risk screening 148

tools for eligibility determination for higher-intensity assessment of geriatric or dementia 149

care interventions. There was variation in how processes evolved over time based on 150

health system resources and patient populations. For example, KPSF has the unique 151

ability to aggregate and analyze patients’ historical records, enabling the creation of a 152

flag that can automatically be populated at triage.13 In addition to this automated flag, 153

KPSF also includes a manual flag for patients who their ED clinicians subjectively think 154

should be eligible for GED care. Similarly, after relying on the Identification of Seniors at 155

Risk (ISAR) tool,17 UCSF has shifted to a “gestalt” frailty assessment question 156

administered by ED triage nurses. All three sites had different approaches with regard 157

to who on the ED care team could direct a patient to GED care. This type of qualitative 158

referral is a recognition of the value of GED protocols, as well as the limitations of 159

standardized instruments in identifying patients who would benefit most from GED care. 160

care needs. The embedded geriatric NP at UCSF plays a central role in conducting a 164

modified comprehensive geriatric assessment (mCGA) and directing follow up care. The 165

UCSF mCGA is a systematic screening of medical, cognitive, and functional capacities 166

which is utilized to create an integrated, patient centered treatment plan that reflects 167

topics important for older adults.18 Meanwhile, KPSF relies on the GENIE role (Geriatric 168

Challenges: 194

Kaiser Permanente San Francisco (KPSF): 195

The KPSF GED team has identified gaps in post ED care regarding confirmatory 196

cognitive testing with Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) after ED discharge. GED 197

leadership has partnered with outpatient care providers, including community 198

paramedicine, neurology, dementia core committee, and supportive care services to 199

continue improving upon follow-up care for vulnerable older adults with abnormal 200

cognitive screens. Continuing to streamline and define the cognitive screening process 201

in the ED remains a significant challenge with the resource loss of the ED Geriatric CNS 202

(after 2024), and is currently a work in process. Like the other ED programs, KPSF GED 203

is unable to directly refer to the memory clinic routinely but can be done in special 204

cases. 205

University of California San Francisco (UCSF): 206

The UCSF AFED team has experienced programmatic challenges related to dementia 207

care and resource connections despite the close coordination with the UCSF MAC. The 208

MAC stopped accepting direct referrals from the AFED Team. Instead, referrals were 209

preferred directly from the PCP for a post-ED follow-up appointment secondary to a 210

potential for intervening medical decompensation. The PCP is notified of the mCGA 211

consultation note with the referral details. 212

Other challenges include the resource loss of the MAC patient navigation 213

assistance and the obstacle of prior authorization with Medicare Advantage Plans. 214

Kaiser Permanente San Francisco (KPSF): 242

Older adults 70+ years of age with an Emergency Severity Index (ESI) score ≥ 2 who 243

were flagged by the GED Screening Score or manually flagged by ED provider or staff 244

were eligible to receive GED care. We considered patients reached by the GED 245

recorded during the ED visit and if there was a GeriCNS or Pharmacist consult note 247

documented in their record. 248

University of California San Francisco (UCSF): 249

Those with cognitive impairment or dementia were targeted for AFED interventions with 250

an AFED consult order (generally patients 65+ with ESI ≥ 2). In general, an AFED 251

consult order occurred when a person was considered frail based on function, cognition, 252

or social connectedness. A consult note from either the AFED pharmacist, social 253

worker, or NP were considered evidence of having been reached by the AFED program. 254

In each case, these notes in the EHR represented not only screening and assessment 255

but also clinical recommendations for care plan improvements. 256

social worker, or physical therapist were considered evidence of having been reached 269

by the AFED program. 270

RESULTS 271

Three San Francisco EDs implemented age-friendly GED care programs to improve the 272

quality of emergency care that persons living with or at risk of cognitive impairment or 273

dementia experience during and after an ED visit. Older adults represented more than 274

30% of ED visits at two hospitals (33% at KPSF, 36% at UCSF, 17% at ZSFG). 275

Populations were diverse in race and ethnicity with White patients ranging from 23% at 276

ZSFG to 50% at UCSF, Black patients ranging from 8% at UCSF to 20% at ZSFG, 277

Asian patients ranging from 26% at ZSFG to 31% at KPSF. Hispanic patients ranged 278

from 8% at UCSF to 25% at ZSFG. Proportion of older ED patients on Medicare Fee- 279

for-Service (FFS) ranged from 4% at KPSF to 81% at ZSFG, yet 86% of KPSF patients 280

were covered by managed care medical insurance. 281

For each ED, a significant proportion of their ED visit encounters made by 282

patients 65+ years of age also had dementia or cognitive impairment histories (14.7% of 283

ZSFG, 25.4% of KPSF, and 23.2% UCSF ED patients had previously diagnosed 284

dementia or cognitive impairment conditions in their diagnosis histories). Of these 285

patients, 17% at KPSF, 39% at UCSF, and 20% at ZSFG received care by their 286

respective GED programs. Resource and staffing availability of each program likely 287

reduced maximal reach of the programs for all eligible patients, whereby even more 288

patients with dementia would have likely received care. 289

Commonalities in GED dementia care programmatic implementation: 290

Screening and Assessment 291

All three EDs use screening and assessment tools to identify patients at risk of cognitive 292

impairment and dementia. All three EDs included delirium and cognitive function 293

assessments. For delirium screening, two used the bCAM, while one used the NuDesc. 294

All utilized the Mini-Cog for cognitive function screening, while one also completed the 295

MoCA, Saint Louis University Mental Status Exam (SLUMS), and Mini-Mental State 296

Examination (MMSE) for cognitive assessment testing. 297

Data Capture 298

Each program captured assessment data in patients' medical records, which is crucial 299

for monitoring changes and maintaining continuity of care. 300

Programs started in different years and have achieved varying levels of GED 306

accreditation in 2021, KPSF achieved Level 1 in 2024, and ZSFG received initial Level 308

Patient Population and Focus 310

KPSF focuses on patients aged 70 and above, whereas UCSF and ZSFG target those 311

aged 65 and above. 312

Resource Allocation and Workflow 313

KPSF employs an automated risk prediction model; UCSF uses embedded NPs to 314

conduct mCGA; ZSFG relies heavily on navigators and social workers. 315

GED Program Reach 316

The reach and capacity of these GED programs vary significantly, with differing levels of 317

patient engagement and service provision based on available professionals and 318

operational hours. 319

DISCUSSION 320

The models of care implemented by KPSF, UCSF, and ZSFG showcase diverse 321

approaches to enhance emergency care for persons living with dementia or at risk for 322

cognitive impairment. Differences by program show how each developed, adopted, and 323

adapted programs unique to the needs and characteristics of their health system, 324

community resources, and most importantly, their patient populations. Each program 325

adopted best practices aligned with the common goal of improving emergency care for 326

older adults, particularly those with cognitive impairment. KPSF stands out with its use 327

of an automated risk prediction model, enabling early identification of at-risk older 328

patients with a GED Screening Score. UCSF benefits from embedded NPs with 329

specialized training. ZSFG leverages navigators and social workers for comprehensive 330

patient support. These strategies highlight the potential impact of tailored interventions 331

based on institutional resources and patient demographics. 332

Across the three EDs, several best practices are commonly implemented to 333

enhance emergency care for patients with dementia. Each program integrates 334

screening and assessment tools designed to identify patients at risk of cognitive 335

impairment, ensuring early intervention and tailored care. Additionally, these hospitals 336

emphasize the importance of data capture, whereby assessment findings are recorded 337

in patients' medical records to facilitate continuity of care and informed decision-making 338

during transitions between healthcare providers. 339

Community engagement is a shared strength among the three programs, with 340

each working collaboratively with local organizations to ensure seamless transitions and 341

ongoing support for discharged patients. All three sites worked with community-based 342

organizations to provide resources for patient post-discharge care, promoting smoother 343

transitions and ongoing support for older adults within their communities. These 344

collaborations underscore the importance of a holistic approach to dementia care within 345

the emergency setting. Collaborations that extend beyond acute medical care are 346

necessary to ensure continuous care beyond immediate medical interventions. 347

All three programs align their efforts to develop interdisciplinary approaches, 348

integrating geriatric medicine, emergency medicine, pharmacy, case management, and 349

social work, among other specialties, to foster comprehensive and sustainable care 350

models. Best practices in geriatric medicine and dementia emergency care models are 351

interprofessional, requiring extensive partnerships to support the care coordination not 352

only within the hospital, but into the community. While there were differences in 353

operational specifics, each hospital creatively utilized community partnerships or 354

programs. KPSF utilized the power of their integrated healthcare system data for 355

patients to develop a screening score. UCSF partnered with the Division of Geriatrics to 356

bring NP consults into the ED. ZSFG created a new role of a non-clinician patient 357

navigator trained to deploy geriatric and cognitive-functional assessments. 358

Despite the best practices, the implementation of these models also presents 359

several challenges. One significant issue is the relatively low number of patients 360

screened, which is in part due to the limited availability of active ED assessment 361

professionals across all programs. This limitation restricts the ability or programs to 362

comprehensively address the needs of all potential dementia ED patients. Furthermore, 363

cognitive impairment and dementia often cannot be diagnosed accurately unless a 364

patient is at baseline, collateral information is available, a decline in functional status 365

can be documented, and a wide differential diagnosis is considered. Nonetheless, the 366

ED setting, despite the challenges of screening and varied professional expertise, may 367

be an important setting for more efficiently recognizing and responding to those with 368

cognitive impairment, especially when integrated with outpatient and community 369

supports. The referral process and supports for post-emergency care is also variable 370

and depending on health system integration of outpatient clinics and permissible care 371

coordination. The ease or complexity of referral processes and care coordination may 372

significantly impact how well older adults or PLWD are able to navigate follow-up care. 373

As GED programs gain traction and demonstrate value, sustainable resources and 374

prioritization of support for such initiatives will advance scalability and broader 375

applicability. While each program has made strides in implementing comprehensive 376

care strategies, there remains a need for more robust data integration systems to 377

streamline processes and improve patient outcomes consistently. 378

Overall, the KPSF, UCSF, and ZSFG programs illustrate the importance of 379

adopting innovative, age-friendly approaches tailored to the needs of patients living with 380

or at risk for cognitive impairment within the ED. The lessons learned from these 381

programs emphasize the value of integrating specialized care models into ED settings, 382

encouraging continuous quality improvement, and fostering community partnerships to 383

enhance patient care. As these models evolve, addressing existing limitations and 384

exploring avenues for resource optimization will be critical in scaling these initiatives 385
